name: Chechen
catalog_quote: Chechen stress is primarily fixed on the first syllable of a phonological word. Stress in Chechen is also often realized by a raising of the tone on a stressed syllable rather than an increase in the intensity (cf English and Russian stress-timed systems).
sweep_summary: Only one title-keyword item exists for Chechen: Komen 2007 (ROA-923), already in our bibliography and already held held by the project (copied into this search of works with stress in the title directory, byte-identical to the live ROA PDF at https://roa.rutgers.edu/files/923-0807/923-KOMEN-0-0.PDF; the old view.php3 landing page is 404). Read in full: main stress on the first syllable of a left-aligned trochaic foot, weight-insensitive, cued by highest pitch; exceptions are preverb compounds (separate prosodic words), list/focus intonation, and inherent high tone on a few suffixes. This confirms the catalog's fixed-strict coding (deciding source Dotton & Wagner 2017, previously confirmed verbatim in the held grammar) and does not supersede it, though it is the stronger first-hand study. Nothing new to acquire from this search of works with stress in the title; the standing list of works to obtain (Nichols 1997 'Chechen phonology', Komen/Molochieva/Nichols 2020 OUP chapter) is unchanged. none were needed for this single-item search.

new_statements.quote: It has been shown that the main stress in Chechen usually lies on the first syllable of the word. Chechen stress uses trochaic feet. These feet should start as much to the left as possible. There is downstep between feet [...]. Inherent high tone on certain morphemes, as well as intonation are able to break up the normal stress assignment pattern. [...] Chechen does not seem to distinguish between light and heavy syllables when it comes to stress assignment.
new_statements.citation: Komen, Erwin R. (2007). Chechen stress and vowel deletion: an optimality theory approach. Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-923, 19 pp.
new_statements.locator: p. 18, sec. 6 'Conclusions' (first-syllable statement); p. 3, sec. 3 (trochaic/leftmost tendencies); p. 19 (weight-insensitivity)
new_statements.reading: First-hand elicitation with pitch tracks: word stress is initial (leftmost trochee, weight-insensitive), realised as the highest tone. Departures are morphological/prosodic, not lexical-contrastive: preverb+verb compounds behave as two prosodic words (preverb stressed separately, per Nichols 1997:966), list/focus intonation adds a final high tone, and a few suffix combinations (e.g. past + question /-írii/) carry inherent high tone that draws prominence to the penult. Consistent with the catalog's fixed-strict coding; if the catalog distinguishes strict from 'fixed with morphological exceptions', the preverb double-stress and suffix-tone cases are the caveats to note.

sources.quote: "In Chechen, stress is fixed on the first syllable. According to Magomedov (2005: 86), long vowels can attract stress away from the initial position, but this view is not shared by other authors. Exceptionally, though Chechen does not have strong evidence for secondary stress, verbs that take preverbs carry stress both on the preverb and on the verbal root (Nichols 1997: 966; Komen 2007a: 8)." Later: enclitic ʔa "can in certain cases attract stress, shifting it to the final syllable of the word (Nichols 1997: 967)"; proclitics t͡sa, ma carry H tone but do not attract stress.
